Three semicircles of radius $ 1$ are constructed on diameter $ AB$ of a semicircle of radius $ 2$. The centers of the small semicircles divide $ \overline{AB}$ into four line segments of equal length, as shown. What is the area of the shaded region that lies within the large semicircle but outside the smaller semicircles?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows a large semicircle with horizontal diameter AB. Inside it are three smaller upward semicircles of equal radius arranged along AB. Their centers divide AB into four equal unit segments, so AB has length 4 and the large semicircle has radius 2. The shaded region is the part inside the large semicircle but outside the three smaller semicircles. The adjacent smaller semicircles overlap, while the left and right smaller semicircles only touch at a point. Reasoning: Model AB as the interval from x=0 to x=4. The large semicircle is centered at x=2 with radius 2, and the three small semicircles have radius 1 and centers at x=1, x=2, and x=3. The large semicircle has area (1/2)π(2^2)=2π. Each small semicircle has area (1/2)π(1^2)=π/2, so the sum of the three small semicircle areas is 3π/2. The only positive-area overlaps are the left-middle and middle-right overlaps. For two unit circles whose centers are distance 1 apart, the full lens overlap has area 2π/3 - √3/2. Since only the upper halves are used, each semicircle overlap has area half of that: π/3 - √3/4. Therefore, the union of the three small semicircles has area 3π/2 - 2(π/3 - √3/4)=5π/6 + √3/2. The shaded area is the large semicircle area minus this union: 2π - (5π/6 + √3/2)=7π/6 - √3/2.
